title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 41-48
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 41-48 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Research work is best handled by an agent rather than a fixed workflow mainly because:
options: The steps cannot be predicted in advance, so the plan emerges from the first searches
The sources are all internal and change only slowly over time
The task has a fixed end state that can be scripted ahead of time
Each request maps to one of a small set of known intents
questions.explanation: Open-ended, path-dependent tasks have no fixed steps to script, so the plan is discovered through the first rounds of searching rather than written in advance.

questions.question: An orchestrator-worker design with parallel subagents outperforms one agent searching in a single window because:
options: Independent context windows let subagents cover different branches in parallel
One very large context window is always cheaper and more reliable than several small ones
Subagents should share a single context window so each can see all the others' findings
A single agent can hold the entire search log and still finish reliably within budget
questions.explanation: Parallel subagents win where a question has many independent branches, because each can work a branch in its own context window instead of one window overflowing.

questions.question: Having a separate verification step for citations, rather than letting the drafting model reconstruct them, matters because:
options: The verification step lets the drafting model write longer, more detailed, and more persuasive reports
A verifier checks each claim against the actual documents instead of the drafter's memory
A verifier removes the need to store or point back to the underlying sources
Verifying citations makes the research run cheaper by cutting the number of searches
questions.explanation: Condensation erodes source fidelity, so attribution should be checked by reading the stored documents rather than reconstructed from a compressed history.

questions.question: How should an agent choose among the ways of observing a web page?
options: Prefer the page's structure when it exists, use a screenshot when it does not, and script fixed steps
Always use screenshots, because images capture the page exactly as a human being would see it in a browser
Always let the model click through the whole page so it can adapt to whatever layout it encounters
Use a script for the steps that vary most and a model for the steps whose path never changes
questions.explanation: Exact element references from the page structure do not drift with viewport size or resolution, while screenshots force the model to infer positions and fixed paths need no model at all.

questions.question: A workflow has ten steps and each step succeeds 90 percent of the time. What is the practical design response?
options: Assume that independent errors will cancel out over many steps, so the whole job still mostly succeeds
Add more automatic retries so the agent can eventually push the overall success rate back up
Collapse steps into atomic verified commands and check the expected result after each one
Accept the drop, because per-step success rates do not affect the success of the whole job
questions.explanation: Per-step success compounds downward across a sequence, so the fix is fewer, verified steps with a check after each rather than a fragile chain of many clicks.

questions.question: Why is a page treated as hostile input in this class of agent?
options: Web pages often load slowly and time out before an automated agent has a real chance to act on them reliably
A page can carry instructions that conflict with the agent's own, and its actions land in live systems
Web pages are always encrypted and cannot be read by an automated tool
Most pages change their layout every time an automated agent opens them
questions.explanation: A page is untrusted input written by someone else, so its text is treated as data and every action is assumed to affect a live system.

questions.question: What gives a coding agent a verifier it can run on its own?
options: Code either compiles or passes tests or it does not, and the agent can run that check itself
A human must review and approve every single edit the agent proposes before it is allowed to continue
The agent guesses whether its change looks correct and then proceeds to the next step anyway
An external service grades the agent's output after each session has fully finished and ended
questions.explanation: A coding agent's success signal is a check that runs itself, such as a test suite or build, so verification is the closing phase of each loop rather than an external human step.

questions.question: What role does the harness play in a coding agent?
options: The harness is the reasoning model itself, and the tools it uses are entirely optional add-ons to that core model
The harness is a second model whose only job is to review and correct the first model's file edits
The model alone can only emit text; the harness supplies the tools and execution environment that let it act
The harness is a fixed program whose behavior cannot be extended by attaching any new tools to it
questions.explanation: The model emits text on its own; what makes it agentic is the surrounding harness of tools, context management, and an execution environment.

questions.question: Why is context treated as the scarce resource in a coding session?
options: Context space is effectively unlimited and cheap to fill, so filling the window faster always improves the agent's accuracy on any task
Every file read and command output fills the window, and quality degrades as it fills, so key information must stay accessible
Context only ever holds the final answer, so it rarely needs to be managed while a task runs
The window resets automatically after every tool call, so it almost never needs any attention
questions.explanation: A session accumulates file reads and command outputs, and model quality falls as the window fills, so keeping the important instructions in view is a design concern.

questions.question: When connecting an agent to a system of record, what should be decided first?
options: Whether each call is a read or a write, since the two paths need separate identities, permissions, and guardrails
Which specific SDK, connector, or API endpoint will be used to physically carry the connection to the target system
Which cloud region or data center the target system happens to run inside
Which language model will be responsible for generating the agent's tool calls
questions.explanation: Reads accept a narrower identity and smaller blast radius than writes, so the two paths need separate identities, permissions, and guardrails and should be designed as distinct integrations.

questions.question: On the read path into a data warehouse, what keeps the agent inside the system's existing governance?
options: Give the agent a raw SQL execution shell so that it can query whatever data it decides that it needs directly
Trust the agent's own prompt to avoid asking for data that it is not permitted to see
Expose a governed analyst tool over semantic views, keep it read-only, and scope it to a least-privileged role
Let the agent read only from a local cached copy of the warehouse tables instead
questions.explanation: The store already governs its data, so the agent should reach it through a read-only analyst tool over governed views and a least-privileged role rather than a raw shell that bypasses those controls.

questions.question: How should the write path into a CRM or ERP be designed?
options: Write directly to the raw database records so that the agent keeps the broadest freedom and operational flexibility
Prefer a governed platform action, and place a human confirmation in front of any destructive or irreversible write
Share the read path's identity and grants so there is only one credential to manage
Skip any confirmation step so that writes can complete as quickly as possible
questions.explanation: A write changes shared business state, so it should go through a governed action that applies business rules and stop for human confirmation when the effect is irreversible.

questions.question: What single resource most determines whether a vector index stays fast?
options: Memory, because the index must fit in RAM or each graph hop becomes a disk read
The total number of rows that the collection happens to be storing at any given time
The number of shards across which the collection has been split and distributed
The size of the client connection pool that the application uses to reach it
questions.explanation: An approximate nearest-neighbor search is a chain of random memory accesses, so when the index fits in RAM lookups stay fast and when it spills to disk latency rises sharply.

questions.question: A vector database backup can meet the database recovery point and still fail the retrieval recovery point. Why?
options: The physical backup was taken just before the final write had actually been committed to disk, so the last record was lost
The restore finished faster than the recovery time objective that the team had previously allowed for
Rows restore cleanly, but search returns stale chunks or mixed embedding versions, so retrieval was not restored
The backup captured the vectors but forgot to capture the operating system state as well
questions.explanation: Database recovery restores rows, but retrieval correctness also depends on the index and embedding model version, so a clean restore can still leave search stale or semantically mixed.

questions.question: What is the consequence of never declaring a consistency model for a retrieval pipeline?
options: The system becomes strongly consistent by default because the index is updated synchronously on every single write
The pipeline is eventually consistent by default, with an unmeasured staleness bound and no monitoring to catch it
The inconsistency window is effectively zero because the vector store acts as the source of truth
Consistency only matters for relational data, so vector search behavior is entirely unaffected
questions.explanation: An undeclared consistency model is still a model: the pipeline drifts toward eventual consistency with a staleness bound that is never measured or watched.

questions.question: Why should raw source records be normalized before they reach the embedding model?
options: Raw payloads waste embedding budget on structural noise and dilute attention, producing low-quality vectors
Normalization allows the embedding model to choose all of its own chunk boundaries directly from the raw source text
Normalization removes the need to chunk the text because the model handles whole documents
The embedding model can reliably separate the semantic signal from syntax without any help
questions.explanation: The embedding model cannot tell meaning from syntax, so structural noise consumes the token budget and pulls attention away from the text that carries the semantic signal.

questions.question: What does change data capture let a retrieval pipeline do?
options: Re-embed the entire corpus on every single run so that the index is always perfectly consistent and current
Replace the embedding model entirely with a fixed set of deterministic rules and mappings
See an event for each insert, update, and delete, so it can re-embed only the content that changed
Avoid needing a vector store at all by serving results directly from the source system
questions.explanation: Capturing change as a stream of insert, update, and delete events tells the pipeline exactly what moved, which is what makes it possible to re-embed only those records.

questions.question: Why must a retrieval pipeline handle deletions as a first-class operation?
options: Deleting a record in the connected source system always removes all of that record's derived vectors automatically
A source delete does not propagate on its own, so without a delete path the removed content stays retrievable
Deletions only matter when the vector store itself is the source of truth for the data
Deletion is handled automatically by the embedding model during the next scheduled pipeline run
questions.explanation: Because the vector store is separate from the source, a deletion has to be propagated explicitly or the derived chunks linger and remain retrievable after the source is gone.

questions.question: Why must an eval harness keep runs consistent, and what is the main thing to pin?
options: So a score difference means real quality change, not noise, which requires pinning the judge snapshot and dataset version
So that individual runs finish faster, which mainly means pinning the batch size and the concurrency settings
So that the application model can be swapped freely between individual runs without affecting any of the reported scores
So that the golden evaluation set can be refreshed automatically from all of the latest real production output after every run
questions.explanation: A score is only comparable to an earlier one if the measuring equipment stayed fixed, so the judge snapshot and dataset version are pinned to keep differences meaningful.

questions.question: How does a capability eval become a regression eval?
options: It is deleted as soon as it begins passing consistently so that the overall suite of evals stays small and fast to run every time
It is refreshed from new production output once each quarter so it stays current
Once it reaches a persistently high pass rate it graduates into the regression suite, where it guards that behavior
It is run only by human graders once it has started passing consistently over time
questions.explanation: A check that the agent has clearly mastered stops asking whether it can do the task and starts asking whether it still does, so it moves into the regression suite to protect shipped behavior.

questions.question: What cost discipline keeps an eval quality gate from being switched off?
options: Run the full LLM-as-judge suite on every single commit so that any regressions are caught as early as humanly possible in the pipeline
Use cheap code-based graders on every commit in CI and reserve expensive judge evaluations for preview and release
Run no automated evals at all and rely on a manual review of a few prompts before every release
Run the expensive judge evaluations only on Fridays so that the overall monthly bill stays low
questions.explanation: A gate that costs real money on every commit is abandoned quickly, so cheap graders run everywhere and expensive judges are reserved for the moments that matter.

questions.question: What three questions does governance exist to answer?
options: Who may change the agent, who accepts the risk when shipping anyway, and how those decisions are proven deliberate
How quickly the agent responds, how cheaply it operates in production, and how many end users it can reliably serve at once
Which model provider is cheapest, which region to deploy in, and which user interface to adopt
How many tokens the agent consumes, how long each run lasts, and how often it retries a step
questions.explanation: Governance covers the accountability measurement cannot supply: who may change a system, who owns the residual risk when it ships anyway, and how that reasoning is documented.

questions.question: How should an AI policy handle routine uses versus hard cases?
options: It should require a review board decision for every single model change so that absolutely nothing can ever slip through the process
It should leave every decision to the individual product teams without any standing rules at all
It should set standing rules so routine uses flow through, and let the board decide only the hard cases that no rule can settle
It should be written once at the start and then never revisited as the organization or its systems change
questions.explanation: Policy exists to preapprove the routine so the board is reserved for the genuinely contested calls; a policy that routes everything to the board just pushes teams to work around it.

questions.question: What keeps a review board from becoming theater?
options: Approving each and every use case that arrives so that absolutely no decision ever escapes its careful oversight and review
Making sure meetings produce decisions, owners, deadlines, and records, while named system owners stay accountable
Restricting the membership to technologists only so that technical risk is always fully understood
Letting the board replace the system owners so that all accountability becomes fully centralized
questions.explanation: A board earns its authority by producing recorded decisions and by leaving a named owner accountable for each system, rather than rubber-stamping or absorbing everyone's responsibility.
